titleEn: To You, LORD, I lift up my soul
progression: | Em Em | Am Am | Em B7 | Em Em |
intro: An alphabetical acrostic: one letter of the alphabet opens each verse, in order, alef through tav. The order is not quite clean. No verse opens with vav and none with qof, resh opens two verses in a row, and a twenty-second verse beginning with pe stands outside the sequence altogether. Twenty-two verses of asking, with a block of teaching in the middle: verses 1 to 7 are petition, verses 8 to 15 turn to the third person and describe the kind of God this is, and then the petition resumes and closes on the whole nation rather than one man. In the Sephardic rite it is the psalm of nefilat apayim, said with the head lowered during weekday Tachanun. Watch two roots recur: the root for waiting and the root for being put to shame.

stichs.en: Of David.
To You, LORD, I lift up my soul.

verses.summary: The psalm opens with a gesture rather than a request. Lifting the soul is the same verb used for lifting the hands or the eyes, so the line is a posture before it is a sentence.

stichs.en: My God, in You I have trusted; let me not be put to shame.
Let my enemies not exult over me.

verses.summary: Shame here is public, not private: it is what happens when the thing you trusted fails in front of people who were watching. That is why the enemies appear in the same breath.

stichs.en: Indeed, none who wait for You will be put to shame.
The treacherous will be put to shame, without cause.

glosses: they will be put to shame
they will be put to shame
verses.summary: The verb of shame is repeated across the two halves with the negative dropped, so the same fate lands on the other party. The private plea of verse 2 becomes a general rule.

stichs.en: Make Your ways known to me, LORD,
teach me Your paths.

verses.summary: The first thing actually asked for is not rescue but instruction. Both verbs carry the object suffix meaning me, and both objects belong to God: Your ways, Your paths.

stichs.en: Lead me in Your truth and teach me,
for You are the God of my rescue;
for You I have waited, all the day.

verses.summary: Teach me arrives twice in two verses, the second time with the conjunction attached. Waiting is named for the first time, and the phrase all the day makes it a duration rather than a mood.

stichs.en: Remember Your compassion, LORD, and Your acts of kindness,
for they are from of old.

verses.summary: The argument is chronological: these things predate the speaker, so they are not being requested as a favour but invoked as a standing fact.

stichs.en: The sins of my youth and my rebellions, do not remember;
according to Your kindness, remember me, You,
for the sake of Your goodness, LORD.

verses.summary: The same verb twice, once refused and once demanded, with the two objects swapped: do not remember those, remember me. The stated ground is God's goodness, not the speaker's.

stichs.en: Good and upright is the LORD,
therefore He instructs sinners in the way.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm and its strangest logic. Goodness would seem to point away from sinners; the verse says it points toward them, and makes that the reason instruction is offered at all.

stichs.en: He leads the humble in justice,
and He teaches the humble His way.

verses.summary: Lead and teach are the two verbs the speaker asked for in verses 4 and 5, now stated as what God does in general. The word for the humble repeats in both halves, the only word held across the parallel.

stichs.en: All the paths of the LORD are kindness and truth
for those who keep His covenant and His testimonies.

verses.summary: Paths and truth come back from verses 4 and 5, but now they are described rather than requested. The second half attaches a condition, which the psalm will spend the rest of its length not meeting.

stichs.en: For the sake of Your name, LORD, forgive my guilt,
for it is great.

verses.summary: The size of the debt is offered as the reason to cancel it, which is not how debts work. The clause makes sense only if the name in the first half, and not the debtor, is what is at stake.

stichs.en: Who is the man who fears the LORD?
He instructs him in the way he should choose.

verses.summary: A question with no name in the answer, so the slot stays open for whoever is reading. The verb of instruction is the one from verse 8, now with an object suffix meaning him.

stichs.en: His soul will rest in good,
and his seed will inherit the land.

verses.summary: The verb is the one for spending the night somewhere, so the promise is lodging rather than possession. What is inherited is left to the next generation, not to the man himself.

stichs.en: The close counsel of the LORD is for those who fear Him,
and His covenant, to make it known to them.

glosses: is for those who fear Him
verses.summary: The highest thing offered in the psalm is not protection but confidence, in the old sense: being admitted to the circle where the plan is discussed.

stichs.en: My eyes are always toward the LORD,
for He brings my feet out of the net.

verses.summary: First person returns after seven verses of description, and the body comes with it: eyes at the top of the line, feet at the bottom, the net between them.

stichs.en: Turn to me and be gracious to me,
for I am alone and afflicted.

verses.summary: The word for alone is the one used for an only child. After the general teaching of verses 8 to 14, the psalm narrows to one person with no one else in the frame.

stichs.en: The troubles of my heart have grown wide;
bring me out of my distresses.

verses.summary: The two halves run in opposite directions: trouble widening, and a request to be led out of a narrow place. The Hebrew for distress is built on a root meaning narrow, so the contrast is spatial.

stichs.en: See my affliction and my toil,
and lift away all my sins.

verses.summary: The verb of forgiveness is the same verb the psalm opened with, to lift. The speaker lifted his soul in verse 1; here he asks God to lift the weight the other way.

stichs.en: See my enemies, how many they are,
and with a violent hatred they hate me.

verses.summary: The same imperative opens this verse and the last one, which is where the acrostic slips. Two objects for one act of seeing: what he has done, and what is being done to him.

stichs.en: Guard my soul and rescue me;
let me not be put to shame, for I have taken refuge in You.

verses.summary: The plea of verse 2 comes back almost word for word, with trust replaced by refuge. My soul returns too, so the closing loops back to the first line.

stichs.en: Let integrity and uprightness guard me,
for I have waited for You.

verses.summary: Uprightness was God's attribute in verse 8; here it is asked to stand guard. The final word closes the root of waiting that ran through verses 3 and 5, now with You attached directly to the verb.

stichs.en: Redeem Israel, God,
out of all his troubles.

verses.summary: The one verse in the psalm with no first person in it. Everything asked for a single life is asked again for a nation, and the word for troubles is the one from verse 17.

pardes.body: Three movements. Verses 1 to 7 ask, and what they ask for first is instruction, not rescue: make known, teach, lead. Verses 8 to 15 stop addressing God and describe Him instead, in the third person, and every verb the speaker had requested comes back as something God simply does. Then verses 16 to 21 return to the first person and to the concrete situation, which turns out to be loneliness, guilt, a net, and enemies. Verse 22 stands apart: no I, no me, only Israel. The teaching block in the middle is not a digression. It is the answer the speaker gives himself before asking again.

The acrostic is the frame and its faults are the interesting part. One letter opens each verse in sequence, though in the first two verses the letter sits on the second word rather than the first. No verse begins with vav, and none with qof: {{18.0}} takes the resh slot, and {{19.0}} repeats resh where qof should have stood. Then {{22.0}} adds a twenty-third line beginning with pe after tav has already closed the alphabet. Readers have long noticed that the three verses standing outside the strict run, the alef of {{1.1}}, the lamed of {{11.0}}, and the pe of {{22.0}}, spell the name of the first letter, which is also the root of a verb meaning to teach. Psalm 34 shows the same missing vav and the same extra pe verse. Whether that is design or the residue of transmission is argued and not settled. Two roots also carry across the psalm: waiting, at {{3.2}}, {{5.8}} and {{21.4}}, and being put to shame, at {{2.4}} and {{20.4}}. Note also {{3.7}}, an adverb that can mean either without cause or empty-handed, and the ambiguity changes who is being described.

Verse 8 is read as the ground of repentance itself: the object of the instruction is sinners, not the righteous, and the verse gives God's own goodness as the reason. On that reading the door is open before anyone knocks. Verse 11 is read the same way, as a claim made on the name rather than on merit, since a debt that is called great is not thereby easier to cancel. The request of {{7.4}}, not to remember the sins of youth, has been read not as a plea for erasure but as a plea about timing: not that they be undone, but that they not be brought forward now. And the psalm's use in Tachanun rests on {{22.0}}, which turns twenty-one verses of one man's trouble into a communal prayer without changing a word of what came before.

The word at {{14.0}} is the one later Jewish mysticism takes as its own name, the fourth level of reading. In this verse it does not yet mean a secret doctrine. It means the close circle where a decision is discussed before it is announced, and the psalm says that circle is open to those who fear Him. The second half of the verse is the point: the covenant is there to make it known to them, so the secret is a thing transmitted rather than withheld. Read this way the psalm's opening line is already the whole method. Lifting the soul, at {{1.4}}, is the raising of what is lowest toward what is highest, and everything asked for afterward, the ways, the paths, the truth, is the route by which the lifted thing is meant to come back down again with something in its hands.
